newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Porsche races to higher profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Porsche races to higher profits.

text.p: German sports-car maker Porsche said on Thursday that it accelerated to unexpectedly higher profit in its 1995-96 business year and would consider resuming a dividend payout for the first time since 1992.
The legendary Stuttgart-based carmaker said it expected to report a profit of about 40 to 50 million marks ($26.2-$32.7 million) for its 1995-96 business year that ends July 31.

Porsche's profit during the first six months of the year totalled 10.3 million marks. The higher profits in the second half were due to cost-saving measures along with strong demand for the popular 911 model, the carmaker said.
Porsche hinted at signs of the strong recovery in January when it said sales were gaining and later said in August that profits would be at least 25 million marks.
But Porsche's profit, particularly when compared to the 1994-95 level of 2.1 million marks, was still above market expectations, analysts said.
"The figures are better than many had forecast and come at a good time since the turnaround is just getting underway," said one Frankfurt analyst who asked not to be named.
Sales during the 1996-97 year rose to about 2.8 billion marks compared with 2.61 billion marks in 1994-95. Porsche said final results for the year will be released on November 6.

Porsche also said its supervisory board would also decide at a meeting on November 6 on whether to resume paying a dividend for the first time since it paid out 2.50 marks for each of its preference shares for the 1991-92 business year.
Preference shares of Porsche rose 13 marks to 1,088 marks while the blue-chip DAX index was down nearly one percent.
The higher profits came in part from increased production of the 911, which surged to 20,132 vehicles from 17,293 in the previous financial year.
The level of 991 sales also reached a new record in the 1995-96 year since the car was first introduced in the 1960s.
Worldwide sales during the 1995-96 year totalled 19,096 vehicles, up from 17,407 vehicles in the prior business year and more than triple the level in 1992-93.
In addition, Porsche said the contract of management board chairman Wendelin Wiedeking has been extended for another five years effective from October 1, 1997.
Wiedeking has been credited with resurrecting the carmaker after it fell to near collapse in the early part of the 1990s following a plunge in the U.S. car market due to the recession.
Under his leadership, Porsche has sharply cut costs and laid out a plan to return to healthly profits by next year which has included scrapping production of unpopular models such as the 928 and 944.
Sales have ironically been strong in America but weak in Germany, where tax laws have hampered luxury vehicle sales.

Part of those plans for greater profitability are pegged to the introduction of the Boxster, which was unveiled this month at the Paris car show and amrked the debut of the first new Porsche in nearly two decades.
The two-seat cabriolet will take its place along side the 911 model as the only two cars Porsche will produce. Porsche also intends to unveil a redesigned 911 in the coming years.
Porsche has seen hefty demand for the vehicle, with orders so far topping 13,000 -- almost equal to one year's production.
"If you want to get excited about Porsche, its about the future and not necessarily about current operations. It's about the Boxster and the future 911," said one analyst.
